transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-01 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Zhou (Redwood SE), Sofia Ramos (Redwood CSM), Priya Menon (OraHealth Head of AI), Lucas Rivera (CTO), Nadia O'Connor (Security Lead), Diego Alvarez (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Discovery on model selection and deployment mode for clinical summarization and live triage; strong PHI constraints; need 32k contexts for long visit histories; tool-calling to internal clinical APIs required; heavy emphasis on security and auditability.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Maya from Redwood, with Ethan on the line. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Priya Menon: Good, thanks. Little rushed but excited to dig in.
[00:18] Lucas Rivera: Hi all, Lucas here. We've been evaluating a bunch of open models and want to understand which make sense for our clinical summarization and triage pipeline.
[00:30] Ethan Zhou: Great. Quick note on agenda — we'll cover model tradeoffs (accuracy, latency, cost), context length needs, multilingual support, tool/function-calling patterns, and deployment options (hosted/dedicated/private) especially for PHI. Then capture action items.
[00:45] Nadia O'Connor: From security side I'll jump in on SOC2, encryption, and VPC questions.
[00:52] Diego Alvarez: I'll bring the ML detail and sample payloads.
[01:10] Maya Patel: Awesome. Priya, could you start with the main use cases and constraints?
[01:20] Priya Menon: Sure. Primary use case is clinical note summarization and real-time triage — we take longitudinal EHR notes, lab results, and patient messages, and surface a short summary + suggested triage action. The big thing is long context — patient histories can be 20k to 30k tokens. We also need Spanish support for ~15% of users. Latency target for triage is sub-1s generation for short summaries, ideally 500-700ms tail for the simple templates. Cost is also a consideration since volume is high.
[02:15] Ethan Zhou: Thanks. So two big asks: 1) long-context models (32k preferable) and 2) multilingual. For model families people look at Llama 2 (variants), Mistral, and some of the newer 32k-capable open models. We also recommend looking at quantization to reduce cost; Redwood's Optimize recommendations can help.
[02:45] Diego Alvarez: We've been testing Llama 2 13B 8k, and a community 32k variant — latency is ok but quality on medical jargon is hit or miss. Mistral variants seemed sharper but cost numbers were different.
[03:10] Priya Menon: Also, tool-calling — we need function calling to query our internal medication reconciliation service and deep-link to charts. So the model needs to support structured tool calling or we use Redwood's function-calling shim?
[03:30] Maya Patel: Redwood supports function/tool-calling patterns and you can do structured output templates. For private deployments we can integrate the tool interface directly with your internal APIs behind the VPC. For hosted we have secure routing options; for PHI use cases most customers pick Dedicated or Private.
[03:55] Nadia O'Connor: Can you clarify what 'secure routing' means? We need clear network boundaries and KMS integration. Hosted is a tough sell unless data is anonymized.
[04:10] Maya Patel: Totally. Hosted can work for deidentified data. For PHI we recommend Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) or Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). Both support KMS/HSM-based key management, audit logs, and SAML SSO + RBAC. We'll share SOC2 and network diagrams.
[04:35] Lucas Rivera: For Dedicated, is the data path tenant-isolated? We need to know about side-channel risks and kernel-level isolation.
[04:45] Ethan Zhou: Dedicated provides GPU pools dedicated to your org with customer isolation at the runtime level and separate storage for KV/cache. For extra control, Private gives you a customer-managed control plane; you own the VPC and keys. There are tradeoffs: Private is more operational lift but gives max control.
[05:15] Priya Menon: Ok that's helpful. On the model side, what's Redwood's recommended starter models for medical summarization and long context?
[05:25] Maya Patel: We usually recommend evaluating a couple: a higher-capacity open model fine-tuned for instruction (e.g., Llama 2 70B instruction-tuned or similar if you can accept compute), and a 13- or 34B 32k variant from the Mistral/Llama families for cost/latency balance. Redwood Verified models include performance profiles we can share. For strict latency/cost constraints, quantized 34B 32k can be a good sweet spot.
[05:55] Diego Alvarez: Is there a maintained 32k Llama 2 official variant? We've seen community forks.
[06:05] Ethan Zhou: Right now, official Llama 2 limits can vary; many community projects provide 32k context windows. Redwood maintains compatibility and will fallback to compatible variants when routing. We'll capture model provenance in the benchmark sheet.
[06:30] Priya Menon: How about hallucination/faithfulness on medical facts? That's our main worry.
[06:40] Maya Patel: Great question. We recommend retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with an embedding store: short pass to retrieve relevant notes, then use the model with that context. Redwood supports embeddings + reranking and you can configure prefix caching (KV cache) to keep common patient data in memory for faster access. Also rollback/QA checks via evals.
[07:10] Diego Alvarez: About KV cache — any limits on size per instance? We have patients with many repeated subsections.
[07:20] Ethan Zhou: KV cache sizing is tunable; runtime manages eviction policies and we can recommend sizes based on your token distributions. We'll ask for a sample of your token length histogram.
[07:40] Nadia O'Connor: Auditing — does Redwood provide per-request logs and token-level cost breakdown? We need immutable audit logs for compliance.
[07:55] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-request traces, token cost breakdowns, and you can stream logs to your audit pipeline; for Private, logs can be kept in your own storage.
[08:15] Lucas Rivera: For latency targets, you mentioned quantization helps. Can you quantify the latency/cost tradeoff?
[08:30] Ethan Zhou: Rough guidance: an int8 quantized 34B 32k model can reduce memory bandwidth and cost ~2-3x vs fp16 while adding small latency overheads depending on kernel support. Our benchmarks can show tail latencies; we can run a 1-week hosted benchmark to measure 95th percentiles with your payloads.
[08:55] Priya Menon: For Spanish and domain-specific terms, should we do fine-tuning or prompt engineering + retrieval?
[09:05] Maya Patel: Retrieval + instruction tuning usually gives the best ROI first. Fine-tuning can help for high-volume, repeatable templates but increases model management. Redwood can run canary rollouts for model variants and help measure quality regressions with evals.
[09:30] Diego Alvarez: We have some sensitive PII and PHI in notes. If we go Hosted for benchmarking, can Redwood guarantee it's isolated and deleted after the run?
[09:45] Maya Patel: For hosted benchmarks we have data handling controls — ephemeral storage and you can request deletion. For production PHI, Dedicated or Private recommended. We'll include deletion SLA in the benchmark agreement.
[10:05] Nadia O'Connor: KMS integration — do you support customer-managed keys and HSM-backed KMS?
[10:15] Maya Patel: Yes, both Dedicated and Private support bringing your own KMS and HSM. We'll share our KMS integration guide.
[10:25] Lucas Rivera: What about model drift monitoring? We need to detect regressions when we change models.
[10:35] Ethan Zhou: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt/eval sets. You can set thresholds and get alerts when a model variant drops below expected metrics.
[10:50] Priya Menon: Any limits around function-calling? We want deterministic structured outputs back to our API.
[10:58] Maya Patel: You can define schemas for function outputs and Redwood supports structured parsing and validation. If the model produces unexpected shape, Redwood can detect and fallback or call a different policy.
[11:15] Diego Alvarez: If we need sub-1s tail latency for short summaries, which deployment is best?
[11:25] Ethan Zhou: Dedicated with reserved latency SLAs is usually best. Hosted can be good for prototyping but tails vary more. Private can be tuned aggressively but requires ops work. We can size Dedicated pools based on concurrency and sequence lengths.
[11:45] Priya Menon: Can you share typical cost estimates for our volume? We process roughly 500k summarizations/month, avg 600 tokens per request, with spikes.
[11:58] Maya Patel: We'll put a model-by-model cost spreadsheet together — hosted per-token pricing, Dedicated commit pricing, and Private licensing. That's part of the spreadsheet we'll send.
[12:15] Lucas Rivera: Are there any customers in healthcare who have done 32k context production?
[12:23] Sofia Ramos: Yes — a couple of early customers use 32k variants in Dedicated/private for long clinical notes, happy to provide references anonymously.
[12:35] Priya Menon: Great. On the technical deep dive, we want to include our infra folks to talk VPC peering, egress rules, and latency to your regions.
[12:45] Ethan Zhou: We'll prepare an agenda and request network diagrams and sample payloads. We'll ask you to share a token-length histogram.
[12:55] Diego Alvarez: One more on retrieval latency — if we embed and store vectors in our infra, can Redwood call our vector DB during generation?
[13:05] Maya Patel: For Private, yes you can host the vector DB and Redwood runtime will call it inside the VPC. For Dedicated we support secure connectors; for hosted we can call a customer endpoint with secure auth but recommend Private for lowest data residency risk.
[13:25] Nadia O'Connor: Any certifications beyond SOC2 we should know — ISO, HIPAA BAA?
[13:35] Maya Patel: Redwood is SOC2; for HIPAA we have enterprise packages and support BAAs for Dedicated/Private customers. We'll flag the legal team to follow up.
[13:50] Priya Menon: That helps. Let's check the timeline — we want a pilot in Q3 to validate model quality and ops.
[13:58] Maya Patel: Sounds good. We'll aim to have the benchmark plan and pricing to you by 6/3 and schedule the technical deep dive for the week of 6/8.
[14:10] Lucas Rivera: One more question — how deterministic are outputs for templated summaries? We need highly consistent output shapes for downstream parsers.
[14:20] Ethan Zhou: You can lock down generation params, use structured templates, and add post-parse validators. If needed, use a smaller instruction-tuned model that is more conservative, or force sampling temp near zero. We'll lay out options in the worksheet.
[14:40] Priya Menon: Ok. Anything else from Redwood side?
[14:45] Maya Patel: We'll also include recommended model list: 13B 8k (fast), 34B 32k quantized (balance), 70B instruction-tuned (highest quality if you accept cost). We'll attach performance profiles and sample latency numbers.
[15:05] Diego Alvarez: Do you support on-the-fly model rollbacks if we see regressions?
[15:12] Ethan Zhou: Yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback to a compatible variant.
[15:25] Nadia O'Connor: Good. On legal side we'll expect the BAA and a secure onboarding checklist.
[15:33] Maya Patel: Noted — legal will follow up.
[15:40] Priya Menon: Great, thanks everyone.
[15:44] Maya Patel: Thanks — recap of next steps: send spreadsheet/docs, schedule deep dive, run hosted benchmark with anonymized data if agreeable.
[15:56] Lucas Rivera: We'll prep sample anonymized prompts and agree the benchmark scope.
[16:05] Maya Patel: Perfect. We'll follow up via email and link in the calendar.
[16:10] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels and minor transcription errors present (e.g., "K V cache" vs "KV cache"), proper nouns might be fuzzy.
